Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
Arthur is a fifty-four-year-old forester who has spent thirty years working the dense woodlands of the Pacific Northwest, a man who knew the language of trees and soil better than he knew his own heart. The event that shattered him happened on a grey November afternoon. He was operating a skidder on a steep, rain-slicked slope, hauling a load of Douglas fir. A choker cable snapped under tension, whipping back with a force he still feels in his bones. It struck his young groundskeeper, a twenty-two-year-old named Caleb, across the thigh, severing an artery. Arthur remembers the sound—a wet, percussive crack—and then the sight of Caleb crumpling, the blood turning the duff a dark, impossible black. He applied a tourniquet, screamed for help on the radio, and stayed with the boy until the medics arrived. Caleb survived, but his leg was badly damaged, and he would never walk without a limp. Arthur was not charged; it was ruled an industrial accident. But Arthur has never accepted that ruling.

In the months that followed, the memory did not fade. When the memory comes, it is not a picture in his mind but a full-body seizure. He feels the exact strain in his shoulders from pulling the lever, the vibration of the machine through his boots, the slickness of the wet bark under his palm. His body locks into that same position, frozen in the moment before the cable sang its terrible song. And with the memory comes a rage that scares him—a hot, blinding fury at the machine, at the company, at the rain, at himself. Then the rage collapses into a grief so heavy it pins him to his chair, a sorrow for Caleb, for the life that was stolen from the boy, for the man Arthur believes he himself has become.

He has come to believe that there is something fundamentally broken inside him, a hidden flaw that caused the cable to break. He cannot rely on himself anymore. He used to trust his hands, his eyes, his decades of experience. Now he knows that his judgment is poison. He is no longer capable of being a forester, the only identity he has ever known. This appraisal has hollowed him out.

His body has become a trigger. A dull ache in his lower back from an old injury will suddenly flash, and he will be back on that slope, the pain of the memory indistinguishable from the pain in his tissue. He cannot walk through the timber yard without seeing Caleb’s face in every young worker’s expression. He has started to avoid the forest entirely, delegating his duties to a junior colleague, spending his days in the office doing paperwork. But even there, he is trapped. Physical proximity to anyone is a threat. When a co-worker approaches his desk, his heart hammers. He watches them closely, scanning their hands, their posture, reading their approach as a potential attack. He knows, intellectually, that he is in a safe place, a quiet office with a coffee mug and a filing cabinet, but he cannot relax. The muscles in his neck stay knotted from the moment he wakes until he collapses into a restless sleep.

At home, his wife, Linda, has grown quiet. She tries to comfort him, but he flinches from her touch. He has stopped going to their son’s baseball games, stopped joining her for dinner with friends. He cannot be around strangers. A man approaching him at the grocery store to ask for the time feels like a confrontation. Arthur watches everyone, searching for the hidden sign that they intend to harm him, because he has learned that harm can come from anywhere, from a simple cable on a simple day.

He finally sought help after Linda found him sitting in the dark garage at three in the morning, still in his work boots, staring at the wall. She asked him what he was afraid of, and he could not answer. He is afraid of the rage, of the grief, of the certainty that he is a dangerous man who should not be trusted with anything or anyone. He is hoping, though he would not say it aloud, that someone can tell him how to live in a world where his own body is a minefield, and where the boy he hurt still limps through his dreams every single night.
